claim: More than half of Virtual YouTubers stop streaming entirely within three years of their first stream, and among those who stop the median career is about 19 months.
stance_target: Content creation has very high attrition within the first three years
scope_conditions: 1,923 VTubers on YouTube, streams observed early 2017 to July 2023; sample drawn from Virtual YouTuber Wiki which lists ~2,800 notable VTubers, so it over-represents established creators and true attrition is likely higher; right-censored for anyone streaming within 3 months of the cutoff
quoted_support: We find that 1,057 (over 50%) have stopped streaming completely within 3 years of their first stream. Of those who fail, the median lifespan is about 19 months.
numbers: median lifespan of those who quit: ~19 months
region: Global; VTubing originated in Japan and the two dominant agencies run Japanese, English and Indonesian branches

claim: Median VTuber career length is 24 months overall, but ranges from 44 months for creators signed to a large agency down to 21 months for creators signed to a small agency, with independents at 28 months.
stance_target: Institutional backing, not talent alone, predicts how long a creator career lasts
scope_conditions: 1,923 VTubers; lifespan defined as months between first and last observed stream; pairwise Wilcoxon signed-rank with FDR correction
quoted_support: The median lifespan of all VTubers is 24 months. Further breaking down by affiliations indicates that the median active period is 44 months for large agencies (Hololive & Nijisanji), 21 months for other agencies, and 28 months for independent VTubers.

claim: A Cox proportional-hazards model gives creators at small agencies roughly twice the risk of quitting compared with creators at the two dominant agencies, while gender and hours streamed do not predict quitting at all.
stance_target: Economic and institutional factors, not effort, drive creator exit
scope_conditions: Monthly panel of 1,923 VTubers; reference category is female creators at Hololive/Nijisanji; several covariates failed the proportional-hazards test and were given time interactions; concordance index 0.680 (sigma 0.023) on 5-fold grouped cross-validation
quoted_support: The risk of failure for independent and other non-large affiliations is at almost 1.3 times and 2 times the baseline risk than those from large affiliations.

claim: Mean monthly Superchat income across VTubers is $2,667 while the median is only $127, a mean-to-median ratio of about 21 to 1.
stance_target: Creator income averages are dominated by a tiny top tier and mislead about typical earnings
scope_conditions: Superchat tips only - excludes memberships, sponsorships, merchandise, concerts and ad revenue; agencies take an undisclosed cut so take-home is lower; 1,923 VTubers, 2017-2023
quoted_support: On average, the monthly income for all VTubers is $2,667. Yet the income distribution is highly skewed, such that the median monthly income is only $127.

claim: One quarter of VTubers received no Superchat income at all during the six-and-a-half year observation window.
stance_target: A large share of active creators earn literally nothing from platform monetization
scope_conditions: Superchat tips only; sample recruited from a fandom wiki of notable VTubers, so the zero-earning share among all VTubers is almost certainly higher
quoted_support: Among all VTubers, only 75% of them had received at least one Superchat, or one fourth of VTubers did not receive any Superchat within the investigated period.

claim: The between-creator Gini coefficient of VTuber earnings rose from about 0.60 in 2018 to 0.75 in 2023, so inequality among creators widened materially over five years.
stance_target: Creator income inequality is increasing over time, not stabilising
scope_conditions: Superchat income only; measured on the same 1,923-creator panel across years, so cohort composition changes as new VTubers debut
quoted_support: the between-VTuber Gini index of VTuber earnings continued to grow from around 0.60 in 2018 to 0.75 in 2023, indicating a rapidly widening wealth gap between VTubers over time

claim: Fewer than 8% of viewers who engage enough to leave a chat message ever pay a creator anything, and over 80% of chatters spend nothing at all.
stance_target: Audience-to-revenue conversion is extremely low even among engaged viewers
scope_conditions: 6.75 million unique viewers who left at least one livechat message; the paper notes the paying share would be far lower if silent viewers were counted
quoted_support: We have aggregated 6.75 million unique viewers, among which 7.96% have sent at least one Superchat and 12.65% have purchased at least one VTuber membership. However, more than 80% viewers in livechats did not spend any money.

claim: Two agencies, Hololive and Nijisanji, capture more than 60% of all VTuber views and more Superchat income than every other VTuber in the sample combined.
stance_target: The creator market is consolidating around a small number of intermediary firms rather than remaining an open individual market
scope_conditions: 1,923 VTubers, 17 billion total views; Hololive n=70 and Nijisanji n=192 creators against 951 at other agencies and 635 independents
quoted_support: These two agencies reap the most views and Superchats on YouTube, more than the total of all other VTubers combined in our dataset.
region: Global; agencies headquartered in Japan with Indonesian and English branches

claim: The single highest-earning independent VTuber earned one-eighth of the top agency VTuber's income and did not place in the top 100 by income, so being unsigned caps realistic earnings even for the best independent performer.
stance_target: Independent creators face a structural earnings ceiling relative to agency-backed creators
scope_conditions: Superchat income only, 2017-2023; single-case comparison rather than a distributional statistic
quoted_support: the top independent VTuber, Kamito, only earned one eighth of the total income of the top VTuber, Kiryu Coco, and was not even among the top 100 VTubers by income

claim: Creators signed to small agencies quit sooner than unsigned independents, which the authors attribute to monetization pressure and burnout outweighing the support that agency backing provides.
stance_target: Commercial pressure is a documented driver of creator exit, distinct from lack of audience
scope_conditions: Interpretation offered by the authors for the observed 21-month vs 28-month median lifespan gap; the mechanism itself is inferred, not directly measured
quoted_support: the pressure to monetize in small agencies might be more likely to cause burn-out and the subsequent dropout for some affiliated VTubers

claim: Income concentration among paying viewers is itself extreme, with per-creator Gini coefficients of viewer contributions around 0.6 rising to 0.8-0.9 as the paying base grows.
stance_target: Creator revenue depends on a handful of high-spending fans rather than a broad audience
scope_conditions: Superchat senders per VTuber; correlation between number of Superchat senders and Gini is rho=0.71
quoted_support: For most VTubers, their Superchat Gini indexes are around and above 0.6, indicating large inequality in viewer spending ... but eventually saturates around 0.8-0.9.
numbers: rho = 0.71 between sender count and Gini

claim: Publicly observable tipping and membership revenue understates top-creator income because Hololive's own financial reporting shows merchandising overtook Superchats and memberships as the leading revenue stream after 2022.
stance_target: Superchat telemetry captures total creator income
scope_conditions: Hololive Production financial report cited by the authors; applies to agency VTubers with merchandising operations, not to independents
quoted_support: Financial report from Hololive Production [23] also suggested that Superchats and Membership were the most important revenue stream until 2022, after which they were only second to revenues from merchandising.

claim: A separate online survey of 34 VTubers found Superchat donations (39.1%) and membership subscriptions (26.1%) were the two most-cited monetization methods, a small-sample self-report the authors use to justify their revenue focus.
stance_target: Establishing which revenue streams matter to VTubers
scope_conditions: Self-selected online survey, n=34 - far too small to be a distributional estimate; cited secondhand
quoted_support: An online survey of 34 VTubers [8] suggested that, among all monetization methods, Superchat donations (39.1%) and membership subscriptions (26.1%) are the two most popular ways.
